# Ānandabhaddekaratta Sutta (MN 132 (PTS MN iii 189))

**ID:** MN 132 (PTS MN iii 189)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Ānandabhaddekaratta Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** Ānanda and One Fine Night
**PTS:** MN iii 189
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Ānandabhaddekaratta Sutta* (MN 132) is the 132nd discourse of the Majjhimanikāya, located in the *Vibhaṅgavagga* [Holz]. Set at Jeta's Grove in Anāthapiṇḍika's Park near Sāvatthī, the sutta depicts the venerable Ānanda instructing, urging, rousing, and gladdening the assembly of monks by delivering the summary (*uddesa*) and exposition (*vibhaṅga*) of the *bhaddekaratta* ("Discourse on an Auspicious Night"), the same core teaching delivered by the Buddha in MN 131 [Holz; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. The verses and their accompanying analysis warn against longing for the past, placing hopes in the future, or being swayed by present aggregates, urging immediate and unrelenting discernment of the present moment [Rogell 2003]. After Ānanda finishes expounding the discourse, he recounts the incident to the Buddha, who fully approves and praises his exposition [Holz; Pande 1974; Rogell 2003].

 DharmaNexus confirms these connections, computing extensive cross-language alignment between MN 132 and the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* (T 26, bundle 43), as well as minor matches in the *Saṃyuktāgama* (T 99) and Tibetan Mahāyāna treatises [DharmaNexus]. Pali-internal text reuse identified by DharmaNexus shows extensive shared passages with the other *Bhaddekaratta* discourses (MN 131, MN 133, MN 134), the *Khandha Saṃyutta* (SN 22), the *Mahāpuṇṇama Sutta* (MN 109), and Abhidhamma treatises such as the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* and *Vibhaṅga* [DharmaNexus]. Scholars have also noted that Sanskrit manuscript witnesses preserve the verses in protective contexts alongside *dhāraṇī* formulas, reflecting potential apotropaic uses of the *Bhadrakarātrī* tradition [Holz; Waldschmidt 1971].
